mainTopic: The war speech's warnings, drashos about גלית and his family, and the enemy champions named in the משנה
overview: This amud finishes the גמרא's explanation of the כהן's speech before battle: the four warnings not to be afraid match four scare tactics of enemy armies. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's mention of גלית and brings many drashos about him. Some explain his name, his boastful challenge, and how his own words predicted his fall to דוד. Others explain why he came morning and evening and stood for forty days, and what the word 'בינים' means. Several drashos describe his mother's immoral life. The גמרא says she was ערפה, also called הרפה. Her four warrior sons fell to דוד, a descendant of רות, because ערפה only kissed נעמי while רות clung to her. They were also a reward for ערפה's four tears. From the way the פסוק holds back from describing גלית's spear, the גמרא learns that we may not praise רשעים, except to show דוד's greatness. Next come רב and שמואל on the Ammonite champion שובך/שופך, a dispute about the 'heaps' of a mighty enemy in ירמיהו, and short lessons about health and worry. The amud ends as the גמרא starts explaining 'ואתם אי אתם כן' with God's name and titles. That sentence finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: Hear the rules of war and go back
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a drasha: the soldiers are told to listen to the rules of war, and those who are exempt go home.
steps.simpleTranslation: Listen to the rules of the battle lines, and whoever is exempt should go back home.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a drasha that started before this section. It explains the speech to the army as 'hear the rules of war, and go back.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the speech has a practical purpose. First the soldiers hear who must fight, and then everyone who is exempt returns home before the battle begins.

keyTerms.meaning: the battle lines, or the rules of war

phrases.english: Hear the words of the rules of war,
and go back.
phrases.notes: This is said to the men who are exempt from fighting; they go home.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a drasha from before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The war speech tells soldiers the rules of war and sends the exempt men home.

steps.title: Four warnings against four enemy scare tactics
steps.stepSummary: The four phrases in the פסוק match four things enemy nations do to frighten their opponents.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the battlefield the כהן says: 'Do not let your heart faint, do not fear, do not panic, and do not be terrified.' These four warnings match four things the nations do: they clash their shields, blow horns, shout, and trample loudly with their horses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the פסוק uses four different words for fear. Each one answers a different scare tactic of the enemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of treating the four phrases as repetition, the גמרא assigns each one a job. Every frightening noise or sight the enemy uses is met with its own warning not to be afraid.

keyTerms.meaning: do not let your heart faint

phrases.english: At the battle, what does he say?
"Let not your heart faint, do not fear,
do not panic, and do not be terrified."
phrases.notes: דברים 20:3

phrases.english: These match four things
that the nations of the world do:
they clash their shields, and they blow horns,
they shout, and they trample.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the war speech
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The four warnings in the פסוק correspond to four enemy scare tactics.
steps.whatToRemember: Four warnings answer four tactics: clashing shields, blowing horns, shouting, and trampling.

steps.title: גלית's name means brazenness against God
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about גלית, and רבי יוחנן explains that the name shows he stood brazenly against הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said the פלשתים came relying on the strength of גלית. רבי יוחנן says he is called גלית because he stood with a bold, shameless face before הקדוש ברוך הוא. He said, 'Choose yourselves a man and let him come down to me,' and 'man' here means הקדוש ברוך הוא, as it says, 'ה׳ is a man of war.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה about גלית. רבי יוחנן explains the meaning of his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name גלית is read as coming from גילוי פנים, a shameless face. The proof is his challenge to send out an 'איש', since the word איש is also used for הקדוש ברוך הוא. That means his challenge was really aimed at ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: relying on his strength as their champion

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִשְׁתִּים בָּאוּ בְּנִצְחוֹנוֹ שֶׁל גׇּלְיָת כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: The Philistines came relying on the strength of Goliath, etc.
Goliath — Rabbi Yochanan said:
He is called that because he stood with a shameless face
phrases.notes: The name גלית sounds like גילוי, which means uncovering, so a face that shows no shame.

phrases.english: before the Holy One, Blessed be He,
as it says: "Choose yourselves a man, and let him come down to me,"
and "man" means none other than the Holy One, Blessed be He,
as it says: "The Lord is a man of war."
phrases.notes: שמות 15:3

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new phrase of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלית's name reflects his brazenness; his challenge to an 'איש' was really a challenge to ה׳.

steps.title: God answers: he will fall by the son of a man
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא responds that גלית will fall by the hand of a 'בן איש', which is דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקדוש ברוך הוא said: 'I will make him fall by the hand of the son of a man,' as it says, 'And דוד was the son of that man from אפרת.'
steps.whatsHappening: This continues רבי יוחנן's drasha. ה׳ answers גלית's challenge to an 'איש' with a 'בן איש'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גלית challenged the 'איש', meaning ה׳. ה׳'s reply matches the wording: גלית will fall by the hand of a 'בן איש', the 'son of a man', which the פסוק uses to describe דוד.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵינִי מַפִּילוֹ עַל יַד בֶּן אִישׁ,
phrases.english: I will make him fall by the hand of the son of a man,
as it says: "And David was the son of that man of Ephrath."
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:12

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הֲרֵינִי מַפִּילוֹ עַל יַד בֶּן אִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יוחנן's drasha about 'איש'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ made גלית fall through דוד, the 'בן איש'.

steps.title: Three times גלית's own mouth trapped him
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר lists three statements in which גלית unknowingly predicted his own defeat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי מאיר: In three places that wicked man's own mouth trapped him. First: 'Let him come down to me,' which pictures himself down below. Second: 'If he can fight with me and kill me,' where he mentioned his own defeat first. Third: he said to דוד, 'Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?' calling himself a dog.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. It shows three times גלית's words hinted at his own downfall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each quote looks like a boast, but the wording works against him. He places himself 'down' in the first, names his own death first in the second, and calls himself a dog in the third.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי מֵאִיר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir:
In three places his own mouth trapped
that wicked man.
One: "Choose yourselves a man, and let him come down to me,"
phrases.notes: "Come down" to me suggests גלית is the one below, as if already fallen.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִידַּךְ: ״אִם יוּכַל לְהִלָּחֵם אִתִּי וְהִכָּנִי וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: and another: "If he is able to fight with me and kill me, etc."
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:9. He mentioned himself being killed before he mentioned winning.

phrases.english: and another, when he said to David:

phrases.aramaic: ״הֲכֶלֶב אָנֹכִי כִּי אַתָּה בָא אֵלַי בַּמַּקְלוֹת״.
phrases.english: "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?"

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה מְקוֹמוֹת לְכָדוֹ פִּיו לְאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new drasha about גלית
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In three statements, גלית unknowingly predicted his own defeat.

steps.title: Didn't דוד speak the same way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: דוד also said 'you come to me with a sword,' so by the same reasoning he should have trapped himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: But דוד also said to him: 'You come to me with a sword, a spear, and a javelin!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the third example. If 'you come to me with sticks' trapped גלית, then דוד's similar words should count against דוד too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sentences look alike, since both say 'you come to me with weapons.' So the גמרא asks why גלית's words count as trapping him and דוד's do not.

phrases.english: David also said to him:
"You come to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a javelin"!
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:45

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the third example in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The third example, 'you come to me with sticks'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: דוד used the same kind of wording, so it should also count as self-trapping.

steps.title: דוד immediately added: I come in God's name
steps.stepSummary: דוד did not stop there; he went on to say he came in the name of ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: He then went on to say: 'But I come to you in the name of ה׳ of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have insulted.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that דוד's sentence is different, because he continued right away and put his trust in ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גלית's statement ended by belittling himself. דוד's statement did not end with the weapons; it ended with ה׳'s name, which turns it into a statement of faith rather than a slip.

keyTerms.meaning: then went on, came back to

phrases.english: He then went on to say to him:
"But I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts,
the God of the armies of Israel,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't. The פסוק itself just says אלהי מערכות ישראל.

phrases.english: whom you have insulted."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the full פסוק in context
steps.terutzHavaAmina: דוד's words are just like גלית's.
steps.terutzMaskana: דוד went right on to mention ה׳, so his words were not a self-trap.
steps.whatToRemember: גלית's words worked against him. דוד's similar words finished with trust in ה׳.

steps.title: Coming morning and evening to stop קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that גלית came out morning and evening to keep the Jews from saying קריאת שמע.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the פלשתי drew near morning and evening.' רבי יוחנן says: he did this to keep them from saying קריאת שמע in the morning and at night.
steps.whatsHappening: A new drasha on the פסוק. The timing of גלית's challenges was meant to interfere with קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק specifies morning and evening, and רבי יוחנן reads that detail as deliberate. Those are exactly the times of קריאת שמע, so גלית's fight was also a spiritual attack.

keyTerms.meaning: to make them stop, to prevent them

phrases.english: "And the Philistine drew near morning and evening,"
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:16

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
in order to keep them from the reading of Shema
in the morning and evening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new drasha on the next פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלית timed his challenges to disturb קריאת שמע morning and evening.

steps.title: Forty days matching the forty days of the Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that גלית's forty days of challenges matched the forty days in which the תורה was given.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he stood forth for forty days.' רבי יוחנן says: this matches the forty days in which the תורה was given.
steps.whatsHappening: Another drasha from רבי יוחנן on the same פסוק. The number forty is linked to מתן תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the timing hinted at קריאת שמע, the number of days hints at the תורה, which was given over forty days. גלית's challenge is read as an attack on the תורה itself.

keyTerms.meaning: and he stood forth, presented himself
in which the Torah was given

phrases.english: "And he stood forth forty days,"
Rabbi Yochanan said:
corresponding to the forty days
in which the Torah was given.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second drasha on the same פסוק as step 8
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלית's forty days of challenges correspond to the forty days of מתן תורה.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן reads both details of the פסוק spiritually: morning and evening point to קריאת שמע, and forty days point to the תורה.

steps.title: What does 'בינים' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק that introduces גלית and asks what the unusual word 'בינים' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And the man of the בינים went out from the camps of the פלשתים.' What does 'בינים' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the פסוק describing גלית going out to fight and asks what the strange word 'בינים' means. This sets up the answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'בינים' is not a common word, so the גמרא wants to know what it tells us about גלית. The word can be connected to 'building' or to 'between', and the answers that follow use both ideas.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'man of the בינים', the title the פסוק gives גלית

phrases.english: "And the man of the beinayim went out
from the camps of the Philistines, etc."
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:4

phrases.english: What is "beinayim"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the earlier teachings about גלית's challenges to explaining the words used to describe him.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word 'בינים' in the פסוק.

steps.title: Four explanations of 'בינים'
steps.stepSummary: רב, שמואל, the school of רבי שילא, and רבי יוחנן each explain 'בינים' differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: he was built perfectly, without any blemish. שמואל said: he was the middle brother. The school of רבי שילא said: he was built strong like a building. רבי יוחנן said: he was the son of a hundred fathers and one dog.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives four answers to what 'בינים' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and the school of רבי שילא read 'בינים' as coming from 'building' (בנין): he was perfectly formed, or as strong as a building. שמואל and רבי יוחנן read it as coming from 'between' (בין): he was the middle brother, or he came from 'between' many possible fathers, because his mother lived an immoral life.

phrases.english: Rav said: that he is built free of any blemish.
And Shmuel said: the middle one among his brothers.
The school of Rabbi Sheila said:
that he is made like a building.
Rabbi Yochanan said:
the son of a hundred fathers and one dog.
phrases.notes: He means his mother was with many partners, so גלית came from 'between' all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Four readings: built without blemish (רב), the middle brother (שמואל), built like a building (דבי רבי שילא), born from among many fathers (רבי יוחנן).
steps.whatToRemember: There are two roots behind 'בינים': 'building' (רב, דבי רבי שילא) and 'between' (שמואל, רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: Why the פסוק says גלית was 'from גת'
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף reads 'מגת' (from Gath) as a hint about the immoral life of גלית's mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'גלית was his name, from גת.' רב יוסף taught: this is because everyone trampled his mother like grapes in a winepress (גת).
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains why the פסוק mentions that גלית was 'from גת'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'גת' is the name of a city, but it also means a winepress, where everyone tramples the grapes. רב יוסף reads it as a hint that his mother was with many men.

keyTerms.meaning: The city גת; also a winepress

phrases.english: "Goliath was his name, from Gath."
Rav Yosef taught:
that everyone trampled his mother like a winepress.
phrases.notes: גת also means a winepress, where everyone tramples. It's a blunt way of describing her immoral life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the words of the same פסוק, building on רבי יוחנן's theme about the mother.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'מגת' hints that his mother was with many men.

steps.title: The written and read forms of 'ranks'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is written 'מערות' but read 'מערכות', and רב יוסף explains what the written form hints at.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'מערות' but we read it 'מערכות' (ranks). רב יוסף taught: the written form hints that everyone had relations with his mother.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a difference between how a word is written and how it is read, and רב יוסף draws a hint from the written spelling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain meaning, 'ranks' of the Philistines, comes from how the word is read (קרי). The written spelling (כתיב) is connected to the word הערה, meaning relations, so it adds another hint about his mother.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written, the way the word is spelled
We read, the way the word is pronounced

steps.confusionAlert: In some places the spelling of a word in the פסוק (כתיב) differs from how it is read (קרי). The plain meaning follows the reading, and the spelling can carry an extra lesson.

phrases.english: It is written "me'arot",
but we read "ma'archot" (ranks).
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:23

phrases.english: Rav Yosef taught:
that everyone had relations with his mother.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching of רב יוסף on the same theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The written form 'מערות' hints that his mother was with many men.

steps.title: Was her name הרפה or ערפה?
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל argue over which name was her real name, הרפה or ערפה, and which one is a nickname.
steps.simpleTranslation: One פסוק calls her 'הרפה' and another calls her 'ערפה'. רב and שמואל disagree. One said her name was הרפה, and she was called ערפה because men came at her from behind. The other said her name was ערפה, and she was called הרפה because everyone threshed her like groats.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא assumes that הרפה, the mother of גלית, is the same woman as ערפה from מגילת רות, and asks which name is her real one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree it is one woman with two names. They only argue about which name is her real name and which is a nickname describing her immoral behavior: ערפה from עורף (the back), or הרפה from הריפות (groats that get pounded).

keyTerms.meaning: The mother of גלית and his brothers
Coming from behind (from עורף, the back of the neck)

phrases.english: It is written "Harafa," and it is written "Orpah,"
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 21:16 and רות 1:4. The גמרא treats them as the same woman.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel:
One said: "Harafa" was her name,
and why is she called "Orpah"?
Because everyone came at her from behind.
And one said: "Orpah" was her name,
and why is she called "Harafa"?
Because everyone threshed her like groats.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from hints about the mother to her actual name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dispute: הרפה is the real name and ערפה a nickname, or the other way around.

steps.title: Proof that 'הריפות' means groats
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings two פסוקים showing that 'הריפות' means crushed grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: 'The woman took and spread the covering over the mouth of the well and spread groats on it.' Or, if you want, prove it from here: 'If you crush the fool in a mortar among groats with a pestle.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the second opinion by showing from פסוקים that 'הריפות' really means groats.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק shows that הריפות is a kind of grain. The second shows that groats are pounded in a mortar, which fits the image of 'threshing' in the explanation of the name הרפה.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says, introducing a supporting פסוק
And if you want, say, introducing a second option

phrases.english: And so it says:
"And the woman took and spread the covering
over the mouth of the well
and spread groats on it."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 17:19

phrases.english: And if you want, say it from here:
"If you crush the fool in a mortar
among groats with a pestle."
phrases.notes: משלי 27:22

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the meaning of 'הריפות' used in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That 'הריפות' means groats, which are pounded.

steps.title: Who were the four sons of הרפה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about four sons born to הרפה and asks who they were.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'These four were born to הרפה in גת, and they fell by the hand of דוד and by the hand of his servants.' Who are they?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק about the four sons of הרפה and asks for their names. This sets up רב חסדא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the גמרא has said who הרפה was, it wants to know which four warriors the פסוק means. It is asking for the names of these four sons.

phrases.english: "These four were born to Harafa in Gath
and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 21:22

phrases.english: Who are they?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues with הרפה, now asking about her children.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The names of the four sons of הרפה.

steps.title: רב חסדא names the four brothers
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא names the four sons: סף, מדון, גלית, and ישבי בנוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: they are סף, מדון, גלית, and ישבי in נוב.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question by listing the four sons of הרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us that גלית had three brothers who were also warriors. Together they are the four the פסוק says fell by the hand of דוד and his servants.

keyTerms.meaning: ישבי in נוב, another of the brothers

steps.whatToRemember: The four sons of הרפה (ערפה) are סף, מדון, גלית, and ישבי בנוב, and all of them fell by the hand of דוד and his servants.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
Saph, and Madon, Goliath, and Yishbi in Nov.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The four are סף, מדון, גלית, and ישבי בנוב.

steps.title: The kisser's sons fall to the clinger's sons
steps.stepSummary: The four giants fell to דוד because ערפה only kissed נעמי, while רות clung to her.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says the giants fell into the hand of דוד and his servants. This connects to the פסוק 'ערפה kissed her mother-in-law and רות clung to her.' רבי יצחק says that הקדוש ברוך הוא said: let the sons of the one who kissed come and fall into the hands of the sons of the one who clung.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why ערפה's four giant sons ended up falling to דוד. It traces the outcome back to how ערפה and רות each parted from נעמי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 taught that הרפה is the same person as ערפה. ערפה kissed נעמי goodbye and left, while רות stayed with her. דוד came from רות, so the descendants of the one who left fall into the hands of the descendants of the one who stayed.

keyTerms.meaning: And she kissed (ערפה kissed נעמי goodbye)

phrases.english: "And they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants,"
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 21:22. This is the end of the פסוק about הרפה's four sons.

phrases.english: as it is written: "And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law,
phrases.notes: רות 1:14

phrases.english: but Ruth clung to her."
Rabbi Yitzchak said:
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
Let the sons of the one who kissed come,
phrases.notes: These are ערפה's four giant sons from the last step.

phrases.english: and fall into the hand of the sons of the one who clung.
phrases.notes: דוד came from רות, the one who clung.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וַתִּשַּׁק עׇרְפָּה לַחֲמוֹתָהּ וְרוּת דָּבְקָה בָּהּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues from the naming of the four sons and explains why they fell to דוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The descendants of ערפה, who kissed נעמי and left, fell to the descendants of רות, who clung to her.

steps.title: Four tears earned four mighty sons
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that ערפה earned four warrior sons as a reward for the four tears she shed over נעמי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא taught: as a reward for the four tears that ערפה shed over her mother-in-law, she earned four mighty men who came from her, as it says, 'And they lifted their voices and wept again.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds the other side of the picture: ערפה did get a reward for crying when she parted from נעמי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק explained why her sons lost to דוד. רבא explains why she had such mighty sons in the first place. Even her small act of crying was rewarded.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that הקדוש ברוך הוא rewards even a small good act, including one from someone who later turned away.

phrases.english: Rava expounded:
As a reward for four tears
that Orpah shed over her mother-in-law,
she merited that four mighty warriors came out from her,
as it is said:
"And they lifted up their voice and wept again."
phrases.notes: רות 1:14. The גמרא doesn't explain here how it counts four tears; it just ties her crying to the reward.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the reward side to רבי יצחק's teaching about ערפה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ערפה's four tears earned her four mighty sons.

steps.title: The spelling of גלית's spear holds back his praise
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is written 'חץ' (half) but read 'עץ' (shaft). רבי אלעזר says this shows we haven't told even half of גלית's praise.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'חץ חניתו' (half of his spear), but we read 'עץ חניתו' (the shaft of his spear). רבי אלעזר says: we have not yet reached even half of that wicked man's praise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to גלית, one of the four sons. It points out a difference between how a word in his description is written and how it is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The written form 'חץ' sounds like חצי, half. It hints that only half of his spear matched a weaver's beam, so the full spear was even bigger. The reading 'עץ' gives a smaller picture, so the פסוק deliberately describes גלית as less than he was.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written (how the word is spelled)
We read (how the word is pronounced)

phrases.english: It is written: "the half of his spear,"
phrases.notes: שמואל א 17:7. It's written with a ח, so it hints at חצי, half.

phrases.english: and we read: "the shaft of his spear."
Rabbi Elazar said:
We have not yet reached half of the praise
of that wicked man.
phrases.notes: He means גלית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the four sons to a detail about one of them, גלית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The written 'חץ' shows that the פסוק did not tell even half of גלית's greatness.

steps.title: We may not praise the wicked
steps.stepSummary: From the פסוק holding back גלית's praise, we learn that it is forbidden to praise רשעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here we learn that it is forbidden to tell the praise of wicked people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from רבי אלעזר's point: if the פסוק held back from praising גלית, we must not praise רשעים either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have described גלית fully but chose a smaller reading. That choice becomes a rule for how we speak about wicked people.

phrases.english: From here we learn that it is forbidden to tell
the praise of wicked people.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכָּאן שֶׁאָסוּר לְסַפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from רבי אלעזר's reading.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is forbidden to tell the praise of רשעים.

steps.title: Then why praise him at all?
steps.stepSummary: If praising the wicked is forbidden, why does the פסוק describe גלית's strength at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then the פסוק should not start praising him at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule it just learned. The פסוק does describe גלית's spear, even if only partly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If praising רשעים is forbidden, the פסוק should have left out the description of his spear entirely. Giving partial praise looks like it goes against the rule.

phrases.english: Then let it not begin with him at all!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule from step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one may not praise רשעים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the rule is true, the פסוק should not describe גלית's strength at all, yet it does.

steps.title: To show דוד's greatness
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק describes גלית only so that we can see how great דוד was for defeating him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is to let us know the praise of דוד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the description of גלית is really there for דוד's sake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not to praise גלית. Showing how strong he was makes דוד's victory more impressive, so that partial description is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: We may not praise רשעים. The פסוק describes גלית only to show דוד's greatness, and even then it holds back.

phrases.english: It is to make known the praise of David.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the purpose behind the praise
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seemed to be praising גלית, which goes against the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The description is there to show דוד's greatness, not to praise גלית.

steps.title: Two spellings of the Ammonite champion's name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about שובך and notes that one פסוק calls him שובך and another calls him שופך.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says the Ammonites came relying on the strength of שובך. In one place it is written 'שובך,' and in another it is written 'שופך.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and points out that the Ammonite champion's name is spelled two different ways. This sets up the dispute in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an implied question here: which spelling is his real name? The גמרא does not answer yet. The next step brings רב and שמואל's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Relying on the strength of (their champion)

phrases.english: "The Ammonites came
relying on the strength of Shovach, etc."
It is written "Shovach,"
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 10:18

phrases.english: and it is written "Shofach."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 19:18

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from גלית to the next champion named in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which name was the real one, שובך or שופך?

steps.title: רב and שמואל on his real name
steps.stepSummary: One says his name was שופך and he was called שובך because he was built like a dovecote. The other says his name was שובך and he was called שופך because people who saw him poured out in fear.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב and שמואל disagree. One said his name was שופך, and he was called שובך because he was built like a dovecote. The other said his name was שובך, and he was called שופך because anyone who saw him was 'poured out' before him like a jug.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל answer the question. Each one picks a different real name and explains the other as a nickname.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like the הרפה/ערפה dispute in step 14. Both agree that one name is real and the other is a description. The nickname is either about his huge size (a dovecote) or about the fear he caused (people poured out like water from a jug).

keyTerms.meaning: A dovecote, a tall structure for pigeons

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel disagree:
One said: His name was Shofach,
and why was he called Shovach?
Because he was built like a dovecote.
phrases.notes: A dovecote was a big, tall structure, so this nickname is about his huge size.

phrases.english: And one said: His name was Shovach,
and why was he called Shofach?
Because anyone who saw him
was poured out before him like a jug.
phrases.notes: A play on שופך: people melted in fear, like water spilling from a jug.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised by the two spellings.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Either שופך was his name and שובך describes his size, or שובך was his name and שופך describes the fear he caused.

steps.title: Heaps of corpses from their arrows
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'אשפתו כקבר פתוח', one opinion says their arrows leave heaps of dead. 'כלם גבורים' adds that they are truly strong, not just skilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says, 'Their quiver is like an open grave; they are all mighty men.' רב and שמואל, or some say רבי אמי and רבי אסי, disagree. One said: when they shoot an arrow, they make heaps upon heaps of dead. In case you think they are only skilled fighters, the פסוק says 'they are all mighty men.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from ירמיהו about a fearsome enemy and gives the first of two explanations. Here the word 'אשפתו' is read as heaps of the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אשפה can mean a heap. This opinion says their arrows pile up the slain. The end of the פסוק, 'כלם גבורים', shows that their success comes from real strength and not only from skill.

keyTerms.meaning: His quiver; here also read as a heap

phrases.english: "Their quiver is like an open grave;
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 5:16

phrases.english: they are all mighty men."
Rav and Shmuel,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי,
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, disagree:
One said: When they shoot an arrow,
they make heaps upon heaps of corpses.
phrases.notes: He reads אשפתו as if it comes from אשפה, a heap or pile.

phrases.english: And in case you say that they are just skilled in battle,
the verse teaches: "they are all mighty men."

steps.triggerLanguage: ״אַשְׁפָּתוֹ כְּקֶבֶר פָּתוּחַ כֻּלָּם גִּבּוֹרִים״. רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion about a different mighty enemy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Their arrows pile up heaps of corpses, and 'כלם גבורים' shows this comes from true strength.

steps.title: Heaps of dung from their huge eating
steps.stepSummary: The second opinion reads the heaps as piles of dung, which show how much they ate. 'כלם גבורים' rules out the idea that they were sick.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other said: when they relieve themselves, they make heaps upon heaps of dung. In case you think it is because they have stomach illness, the פסוק says 'they are all mighty men.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second opinion on the same פסוק. It reads 'אשפתו' as heaps of waste rather than heaps of dead bodies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Huge piles of waste mean they eat enormous amounts, the way mighty warriors do. 'כלם גבורים' shows this comes from their strength and not from illness.
steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions read 'אשפתו' as heaps, either of corpses or of dung. Both use 'כלם גבורים' to show that these enemies were truly mighty.

phrases.english: And one said: When they take care of their needs,
they make heaps upon heaps of dung.

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר מִפְּנֵי שֶׁחוֹלֵי מֵעַיִים הֵם
phrases.english: And in case you say it is because they are sick in their intestines,
the verse teaches: "they are all mighty men."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second side of the dispute begun in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The heaps are dung from their huge eating, and 'כלם גבורים' shows they were strong, not sick.

steps.title: Too much waste is a sign of intestinal illness
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי infers from the dung opinion that a person with abundant excrement has an intestinal illness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי said: Learn from this that someone whose excrement is abundant has an illness of the intestines.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי takes the second opinion from the last step, that the heaps were dung, and draws a medical lesson from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That opinion needed 'כלם גבורים' to show the soldiers were not sick. רב מרי reasons that if the פסוק had to rule out sickness, then a lot of waste normally does point to illness. So he concludes that abundant excrement is a sign of a stomach or intestinal problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this; a conclusion drawn from what was just said

phrases.english: Rav Mari said: Learn from this:
phrases.notes: 'This' is the last opinion: the heaps were dung, and 'כלם גבורים' shows they weren't sick.

phrases.english: one whose excrement is abundant,
has an illness of the intestines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical inference from the dung opinion in Step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Abundant excrement is a sign of an intestinal illness.

steps.title: Why does it matter to know this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference רב מרי's observation makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we need to know that a lot of waste means illness. It is setting up the practical answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A medical fact sounds like it has nothing to do with Torah learning. So the גמרא wants to know what a person is actually supposed to do with this knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: What difference does it make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical use of רב מרי's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical result follows from knowing that abundant excrement signals illness.

steps.title: So the person will take care of himself
steps.stepSummary: The practical point is that such a person should get himself treated.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that he will take care of himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the point is practical: someone who sees this sign in himself should look after his health.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing the sign lets a person notice the problem early. Then he can act and get it treated instead of ignoring it.

keyTerms.meaning: He should take the trouble to care for himself

steps.whatToRemember: רב מרי's lesson from the פסוק: abundant waste signals intestinal illness, so a person who notices it should get treatment.

phrases.english: So that he will take care of himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The person should take the trouble to treat himself.

steps.title: What to do with worry in your heart
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי read 'ישחנה' in משלי two ways: push the worry out of your mind, or talk it over with others.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If there is worry in a man's heart, ישחנה.' רבי אמי and רבי אסי disagree. One says: he should push it out of his mind. The other says: he should talk about it with others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another piece of advice about taking care of yourself, this time for worry, and gives two readings of one word in a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ישחנה is read with different sounds. One reading, ישׂחנה, means remove it, so a person should put the worry out of his mind. The other, ישׂיחנה, means speak it, so he should share his worry with other people.

keyTerms.meaning: He should push it out of his mind
He should talk it over with others

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions agree that a person should deal with worry and not just carry it. They only disagree about how: forget it, or talk it out.

phrases.english: 'If there is worry in a man's heart, let him bend it,'
phrases.notes: משלי 12:25. The word ישחנה is unclear, and the two opinions read it two different ways.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi disagree.
One said: he should push it out of his mind,
and one said: he should talk about it with others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related piece of advice about caring for oneself, now for worry instead of the body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worried person should either put the worry out of his mind or share it with others.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק describe God's help at such length?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's words 'ואתם אי אתם כן' and asks why the פסוק spells out God's presence in battle so fully.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'But you are not like them, etc.' Why all of this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the כהן's speech in the משנה and asks why the פסוק uses so many words to describe God going with the army. It is setting up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says God 'goes with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.' It could have said this more briefly. So the גמרא asks why it gives such a long description.

keyTerms.meaning: But you are not like them

phrases.english: 'But you are not like them, etc.'
phrases.notes: This quotes the כהן's speech in the משנה, which goes on with דברים 20:4.

phrases.english: And why all of this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side lessons and goes back to explaining the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the פסוק goes into so much detail about God accompanying the army.

steps.title: The answer begins: because of God's name and all His titles
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer that the reason has to do with God's name and all His titles. The sentence continues on the next lines.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the name of God and all His titles...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer to why the פסוק says so much. The sentence is not finished here and goes on in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer ties the long wording to the presence of God's name and all His titles. The rest of the sentence, which explains where these are and how they go with the army, comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: His titles, the other names used for God

phrases.english: Because the name of God and all His titles

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of Step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer, still in progress, connects the long wording to God's name and all His titles.
